title: Seven deadly sins
description: Set of vices in Christian theology
wiki_lead:
The seven deadly sins (also known as the capital vices or cardinal sins) function as a grouping of major vices within the teachings of Christianity. They are not explicitly listed in the Bible but developed within early Christian theological tradition, drawing on various biblical passages. In the standard list, the seven deadly sins according to the Catholic Church are wrath, greed, pride, envy, sloth, lust, and gluttony.
In Catholicism, the classification of deadly sins into a group of seven originated with Tertullian and continued with Evagrius Ponticus. The concepts were partly based on Greco-Roman and Biblical antecedents. Later, the concept of seven deadly sins evolved further, as shown by historical context based on the Latin language of the Roman Catholic Church, though with significant influence from the Greek language and associated religious traditions. Knowledge of this concept is evident in various treatises; in paintings and sculpture (for example, architectural decorations on churches in some Catholic parishes); and in some older textbooks. Further knowledge has been derived from patterns of confession.
During later centuries and in modern times, the idea of sins (especially seven in number) has influenced or inspired various streams of religious and philosophical thought, fine art painting, and modern popular media such as literature, film, and television.

History

With reference to the seven deadly sins, "evil thoughts" can be categorized as follows:

physical (thoughts produced by the nutritive, sexual, and acquisitive appetites)
emotional (thoughts produced by depressive, irascible, or dismissive moods)
mental (thoughts produced by jealous, boastful, or hubristic states of mind)
The fourth-century monk Evagrius Ponticus reduced the logismoi (or forms of temptation) from nine to eight in number, as follows:

Γαστριμαργία (gastrimargia) gluttony
Πορνεία (porneia) prostitution, fornication
Φιλαργυρία (philargyria) greed
Λύπη (lypē) sadness, rendered in the Philokalia as envy, sadness at another's good fortune
Ὀργή (orgē) wrath
Ἀκηδία (akēdia) acedia (apathy, neglect, or indifference), rendered in the Philokalia as dejection
Κενοδοξία (kenodoxia) boasting
Ὑπερηφανία (hyperēphania) pride, sometimes rendered as self-overestimation, arrogance, or grandiosity
Evagrius's list was translated into their Latin equivalents in the genitive singular in many writings of John Cassian, one of Evagrius’s students; the list thus became part of the Western tradition's spiritual pietas or Catholic devotions as follows:

Gula (gluttony)
Fornicatio (lust, fornication)
Avaritia (greed, avarice)
Tristitia (sorrow, despair, despondency)
Ira (wrath)
Acedia (sloth)
Vanagloria (vanity, vainglory)
Superbia (pride)

grok_lead: The seven deadly sins, also known as the capital vices or cardinal sins, are a traditional set of principal vices in Christian theology that are viewed as especially harmful to the soul because they engender further wrongdoing and spiritual corruption. These sins are typically enumerated as pride (self-exaltation), greed (or avarice; excessive pursuit of wealth), lust (improper sexual desire), envy (resentment of others' possessions), gluttony (overindulgence in food), wrath (or anger; uncontrolled anger), and sloth (or acedia; spiritual laziness). Originating in early Christian monastic practices, the concept traces back to the fourth-century Egyptian ascetic Evagrius Ponticus, who outlined eight "evil thoughts" or temptationsâ gluttony, lust, avarice, sadness, acedia, anger, vainglory, and pride âto guide monks away from spiritual pitfalls. These ideas were transmitted to the Western Church by John Cassian in the early fifth century through his writings on desert monasticism. In the late sixth century, Pope Gregory I refined the list in his Moralia in Job, consolidating it into seven by combining vainglory with pride, eliminating sadness, and introducing envy, while designating pride as the root of all sin. The framework was further elaborated in the thirteenth century by Thomas Aquinas in his Summa Theologica, where he emphasized their role in fostering other vices and contrasted them with the seven virtues as aids to moral formation. Though not explicitly biblical, the sins draw from scriptural themes of human frailty and have profoundly influenced Christian ethics, art, literature, and moral instruction across centuries, serving as a diagnostic tool for confession and self-examination in Catholic and broader Christian traditions. While the seven deadly sins are traditionally regarded as vices harmful to the soul in Christian theology, some contemporary self-help, business, and secular literature reframes or channels them positively as potential drivers of personal success, productivity, and wealth accumulation. A key example is the 2002 book Sin to Win: Seven Deadly Steps to Success by Marc Lewis, which provides practical advice on productively applying each sin to achieve personal and professional goals. Similarly, some commentators argue that traits associated with these sins, such as greed and envy, can motivate innovation and invention, while sloth inspires labor-saving technologies.
